solution.concept_anchor: Project Tiger legal basis under WLPA 1972
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because many students associate Project Tiger with a dedicated standalone law, making the 'Project Tiger Act' option plausible to those who have not verified the actual legislative basis.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): No standalone 'Project Tiger Act' exists — Project Tiger was launched as an administrative scheme, not under separate legislation.
Eliminate (c): Project Tiger was launched in 1973, well before the Environment Protection Act 1986 came into existence.
Eliminate (d): The Forest Conservation Act 1980 governs diversion of forest land, not wildlife conservation schemes like Project Tiger.
Confirm (b): Project Tiger was launched in 1973 under the framework of the Wildlife Protection Act 1972 — the correct answer is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students familiar with conservation legislation often assume that a scheme as significant as Project Tiger must have its own dedicated statute. The trap here exploits this assumption by placing 'Project Tiger Act' as the first option. The Wildlife Protection Act 1972 is the correct parent legislation, but since NTCA was added much later via the 2006 amendment, students sometimes conflate the launch of Project Tiger with the statutory framework that came 33 years afterward.
solution.final_explanation:
Project Tiger was launched in April 1973 as an administrative scheme of the Government of India, operating under the broad framework of the Wildlife Protection Act 1972 — it was not backed by any standalone legislation at inception.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: No 'Project Tiger Act' exists. The scheme relied on administrative directives and the WLPA framework.
• Option (b) — Correct: The Wildlife Protection Act 1972 provided the foundational legal framework under which tiger habitats could be designated and protected.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The Environment Protection Act 1986 was enacted over a decade after Project Tiger's launch and addresses a broader range of environmental concerns.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The Forest Conservation Act 1980 regulates diversion of forest land for non-forest purposes — it is not the basis for wildlife conservation schemes.

Value Addition:
• Project Tiger received statutory institutional backing only in 2006, when Chapter IVB was inserted into the WLPA via amendment, creating NTCA.
• The gap between 1973 (launch) and 2006 (statutory backing) is 33 years — a classic UPSC time-gap trap.
• As of 2023, India has approximately 54 Tiger Reserves spread across 18 states.

solution.concept_anchor: NTCA statutory status and Project Tiger timeline

statement_analysis.statement: The National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA) was established simultaneously with the launch of Project Tiger in 1973.
statement_analysis.reason: Project Tiger was launched in 1973 as an administrative scheme; NTCA was created only through the WLPA Amendment of 2006 (Chapter IVB), 33 years later.

statement_analysis.statement: NTCA is a statutory body whose establishment derives from the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972.
statement_analysis.reason: NTCA was established under Section 38L of the WLPA 1972, inserted via the Wildlife Protection (Amendment) Act 2006 — it is a statutory, not constitutional, body.

statement_analysis.statement: The Chairperson of NTCA is the Minister of Environment, Forest and Climate Change.
statement_analysis.reason: Under Section 38L, NTCA is chaired by the Minister in charge of Environment, Forest and Climate Change; the Minister of State serves as Vice-Chairperson.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is deceptive because students who correctly identify Statements 2 and 3 as true may also incorrectly accept Statement 1, assuming NTCA and Project Tiger share a common origin.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is false: NTCA was created in 2006 via WLPA Amendment, not in 1973 alongside Project Tiger — this eliminates options (a) and (d).
Statement 2 is correct: NTCA derives its authority from Section 38L of WLPA 1972 — this keeps option (c) in play.
Statement 3 is correct: The MoEFCC Minister chairs NTCA as per the statutory provision — confirms option (c).
Only Statements 2 and 3 are correct — the answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap in Statement 1 exploits a very common confusion: because Project Tiger eventually became the institutional precursor to NTCA, students assume both were established together. The 33-year gap between 1973 and 2006 is the critical fact that distinguishes a historically-aware student from one relying on surface-level association.
solution.final_explanation:
Project Tiger and NTCA are frequently collapsed into a single institutional origin story, but they are separated by over three decades of administrative history.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: NTCA came into existence only after the 2006 amendment to WLPA. Prior to that, Project Tiger was run as an administrative scheme under the Forest Department without a dedicated statutory authority.
• Statement 2 — Correct: NTCA is a statutory body created under Section 38L of WLPA 1972 (as amended in 2006). It is NOT a constitutional body — an important distinction for UPSC.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The WLPA specifies that the Union Minister for Environment, Forest and Climate Change chairs NTCA, making it a ministerially-headed statutory authority.

Value Addition:
• NTCA shifted tiger conservation from Forest Department control to a dedicated, minister-headed statutory body.
• NTCA can recommend withdrawal of Tiger Reserve status — a power distinct from the CEC's supervisory role.
• The 2006 amendment also introduced Chapter IVB, which codified Tiger Conservation Plans as mandatory instruments.

solution.concept_anchor: Tiger Reserve declaration process under WLPA Section 38V

statement_analysis.statement: A Tiger Reserve in India is declared by the Central Government upon a recommendation from the NTCA.
statement_analysis.reason: Tiger Reserves are declared by the respective State Government (not Central Government) on the recommendation of NTCA under Section 38V of WLPA 1972.

statement_analysis.statement: The Core Zone of a Tiger Reserve is legally designated as the Critical Tiger Habitat where co-existence with human activity is strictly prohibited.
statement_analysis.reason: The Core Zone is synonymous with the Critical Tiger Habitat (CTH) under Section 38V(4), and it is treated as inviolate — no human activity other than conservation is permitted.

statement_analysis.statement: A Tiger Reserve and the National Park or Wildlife Sanctuary within the same area carry identical legal designations under the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972.
statement_analysis.reason: Tiger Reserve, National Park, and Wildlife Sanctuary are three distinct legal designations under WLPA 1972; overlapping boundaries are common but each retains its own separate legal status and management rules.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because students may only identify Statement 1 as incorrect and overlook Statement 3, which tests a subtler distinction between overlapping but legally separate designations.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is incorrect: Declaration is by the State Government, not the Central Government — eliminating options where only Statement 3 is flagged.
Statement 2 is correct: CTH (Core Zone) inviolability is a statutory feature of Tiger Reserves — this means Statement 2 cannot be in the 'incorrect' category.
Statement 3 is incorrect: Tiger Reserve, National Park, and Wildlife Sanctuary are legally distinct designations even when spatially overlapping.
Statements 1 and 3 are NOT correct — the answer is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 exploits the natural assumption that a nationally significant designation like a Tiger Reserve must be declared by the Central Government. The actual law vests this power in State Governments, subject to NTCA recommendation — a federal design students often invert. Statement 3 exploits the common confusion arising from overlapping boundaries: Corbett Tiger Reserve, for instance, encompasses Jim Corbett National Park, leading students to treat the designations as legally equivalent.
solution.final_explanation:
The legal architecture of Tiger Reserves under WLPA 1972 involves multiple actors and must not be conflated with other protected area categories.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Under Section 38V of WLPA 1972, it is the State Government that declares a Tiger Reserve, acting on NTCA's recommendation. The Central Government does not make this declaration.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Core Zone equals the Critical Tiger Habitat (CTH). Section 38V(4) mandates that CTH be maintained as inviolate — no human use except conservation activities is permitted.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Overlapping geography does not merge legal designations. A Tiger Reserve may contain a National Park or Wildlife Sanctuary, but each designation carries different legal rules for management, permissible activities, and declaration authority.

Value Addition:
• Buffer zones around Tiger Reserves allow regulated co-existence and eco-tourism, unlike core zones.
• As of 2023, India has approximately 54 Tiger Reserves in 18 states.
• The distinction between CTH and buffer zone is critical for questions on tribal rights and relocation.

solution.concept_anchor: CTH notification and FRA 2006 tribal rights reconciliation

statement_analysis.statement: Critical Tiger Habitat (CTH) is defined under Section 38V(4) of the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972 as areas where co-existence between tigers and human communities is scientifically deemed impossible.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 38V(4) defines CTH precisely on this criterion — it is not a blanket designation but one based on scientific assessment of co-existence feasibility.

statement_analysis.statement: Notification of an area as Critical Tiger Habitat automatically extinguishes all forest rights of tribal communities recognized under the Forest Rights Act, 2006.
statement_analysis.reason: Supreme Court interpretations (consistent with Niyamgiri-type precedents) hold that FRA 2006 rights cannot be extinguished merely by CTH notification; relocation must be voluntary with Gram Sabha consent.

statement_analysis.statement: Relocation of communities from CTH areas requires the free, prior, and informed consent of the affected communities as mandated by the Forest Rights Act, 2006.
statement_analysis.reason: FRA 2006 and its rules explicitly require voluntary relocation with free, prior, informed consent — coercive displacement is legally impermissible post-FRA.

statement_analysis.statement: The compensation package for families relocated from Tiger Reserve core zones has been standardized at a minimum of Rs. 10 lakh per family across all states under a Central statute.
statement_analysis.reason: The Rs. 10 lakh figure is an NTCA advisory guideline, not a mandate under any Central statute. States may offer different packages; there is no uniform national compensation law.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because students who correctly identify Statements 1 and 3 as true may also accept Statement 4 as statutory, confusing NTCA advisory guidelines with binding legal provisions.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct: Section 38V(4) defines CTH on the basis of co-existence impossibility — a precise statutory criterion.
Statement 2 is incorrect: CTH notification does not extinguish FRA rights; voluntary relocation with Gram Sabha consent is mandatory.
Statement 3 is correct: FRA 2006 mandates free, prior, informed consent for any relocation from forest areas.
Statement 4 is incorrect: The Rs. 10 lakh figure is an advisory guideline, not a statutory mandate — only two statements (1 and 3) are correct, so the answer is (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is a classic scope-extension trap: students who know CTH is legally inviolate may assume that this inviolability overrides FRA rights — but courts have consistently held that both laws must be reconciled and that CTH notification alone cannot extinguish FRA-recognized rights. Statement 4 traps students who recall the Rs. 10 lakh figure but do not know its source (advisory vs. statutory).
solution.final_explanation:
The intersection of WLPA 1972 and Forest Rights Act 2006 in CTH management is one of the most legally nuanced areas tested in UPSC.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Section 38V(4) provides the statutory definition of CTH based on scientific assessment of co-existence feasibility.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: CTH notification does not automatically extinguish FRA rights. Courts have held that the two laws must operate together; involuntary displacement is legally impermissible.
• Statement 3 — Correct: FRA 2006 mandates free, prior, informed consent before any relocation — this requirement applies even within the inviolate CTH.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: The Rs. 10 lakh compensation figure is an NTCA advisory/guideline, not a statutory entitlement created by Central legislation. Only Statements 1 and 3 are correct.

Value Addition:
• The tension between WLPA 1972 and FRA 2006 reflects a broader constitutional question about balancing conservation and tribal rights.
• Gram Sabha consent is the procedural safeguard under FRA — bypassing it renders relocation legally vulnerable.
• NTCA issues advisory circulars on compensation packages, but enforcement rests with state governments.

solution.concept_anchor: WCCB, NTCA, WII — distinct mandates under MoEFCC
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) swaps the CITES coordination role between NTCA and WCCB, which trips students who associate NTCA with all international treaty matters related to tigers.
elimination_logic: WCCB handles enforcement and intelligence on wildlife crime, and is India's CITES coordination agency — matches with description 3.
NTCA is the statutory body approving Tiger Conservation Plans and monitoring tiger reserves — matches with description 1.
WII is the autonomous research institute in Dehradun conducting the All-India Tiger Estimation and landscape planning — matches with description 4.
Global Tiger Forum is the intergovernmental body with its secretariat in New Delhi that India is a member of — matches with description 2. This gives A-3, B-1, C-2, D-4 — option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The most dangerous swap in this question is between WCCB and NTCA regarding CITES coordination. Students naturally associate NTCA with all international tiger-related commitments since it is the apex statutory body for tiger conservation. However, CITES implementation in India — including trade permits, seizure records, and international reporting — is handled by WCCB, not NTCA. This entity-swap is the most commonly tested distinction in this domain.
solution.final_explanation:
Four bodies operate in the tiger conservation ecosystem under MoEFCC, each with a clearly distinct mandate that UPSC regularly tests through match-column and direct questions.

Correct matches: A-3, B-1, C-2, D-4

• WCCB (A) — Description 3: WCCB is the statutory enforcement agency for wildlife crime intelligence and is India's designated authority for CITES implementation. It is NOT tiger-specific.
• NTCA (B) — Description 1: NTCA approves Tiger Conservation Plans, monitors tiger reserves, and provides policy guidance to state governments. It holds statutory authority under WLPA.
• Global Tiger Forum (C) — Description 2: GTF is an intergovernmental body promoting tiger conservation globally; India is a founding member and its secretariat is located in New Delhi.
• WII (D) — Description 4: WII, an autonomous institute under MoEFCC based in Dehradun, conducts the All-India Tiger Estimation every 4 years in collaboration with NTCA and states.

Value Addition:
• WCCB was established in 2007 — after the 2006 WLPA amendment that also created NTCA.
• WII is NOT a statutory body — it is an autonomous research institution; this legal character distinction frequently appears in MCQs.
• Forest Survey of India (FSI) assesses forest cover, not wildlife populations — a common conflation with WII.

solution.concept_anchor: Buffer Zone vs. ESZ — different legal instruments
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because students who know both statements are factually true may assume a causal link exists, not realising that Buffer Zones and ESZs are declared under entirely different legal instruments and that one does not create the other.
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is A correct? Yes. Buffer Zones under WLPA 1972 allow regulated human use, tourism, and community conservation activities — this is factually accurate.
Step 2 — Is R correct? Yes. ESZs are declared by MoEFCC under the Environment Protection Act 1986 and are separate notifications around Protected Areas — factually accurate.

Step 3 — Does R explain A? No. The existence of ESZs as a separate EPA 1986 instrument does NOT explain why Buffer Zones permit regulated human use under WLPA 1972. These are parallel but legally independent mechanisms; R does not cause or explain the co-existence model of Buffer Zones.
Both A and R are correct but R does NOT explain A — the answer is (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This question exploits a spatial conflation trap: because Buffer Zones and ESZs often overlap geographically around Protected Areas, students treat them as legally interconnected. In fact, Buffer Zones are created under WLPA 1972 as part of Tiger Reserve zoning, while ESZs are separately notified under the Environment Protection Act 1986 by MoEFCC. One does not derive from the other, and the regulatory rules governing each are distinct — making R factually true but causally irrelevant to A.
solution.final_explanation:
The distinction between Buffer Zones and Eco-Sensitive Zones is one of the most frequently tested conceptual separations in the conservation topic.

Assertion (A) is correct: Buffer Zones under Section 38V of WLPA 1972 are designed around a co-existence model — regulated eco-tourism, community conservation activities, and sustainable use are all permitted, unlike the inviolate Core/CTH.

Reason (R) is correct: ESZs are separately notified by MoEFCC under the Environment Protection Act 1986 around National Parks, Wildlife Sanctuaries, and other Protected Areas. A 2022 Supreme Court ruling required a minimum 1 km ESZ around National Parks and Sanctuaries.

Causal relationship: R does NOT explain A. The Buffer Zone co-existence model flows from WLPA 1972 zoning design, not from the existence of ESZs under EPA 1986. They are parallel legal instruments that may overlap spatially but are independently operative.

Value Addition:
• ESZ is NOT automatically mandated around Tiger Reserves — it applies to National Parks and Wildlife Sanctuaries.
• An ESZ and a Buffer Zone can geographically coincide but follow different rules under different parent laws.
• SC's 2022 ESZ ruling sparked controversy in states like Kerala where ESZ boundaries affected local communities.

solution.concept_anchor: All-India Tiger Estimation methodology evolution
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is deceptive because students may believe camera traps replaced pugmarks only after the Sariska crisis (2004-05) came to light, placing the methodology change after the crisis rather than understanding it as part of the broader WII-led scientific evolution.
elimination_logic: Project Tiger was launched in 1973 — this is the earliest event and must come first in any correct sequence.
The Sariska local extinction was confirmed around 2004-05 — this predates the formal 2006 WLPA amendment that created NTCA.
The WLPA Amendment 2006 establishing NTCA came after the Sariska crisis, which was a direct institutional trigger for the reform.
The 2022 All-India Tiger Estimation (confirming ~3,682 tigers) is the most recent event — correct sequence is 1973 → 2004-05 → 2006 → 2022, matching option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The chronological trap here targets students who know all four events individually but are uncertain about whether the 2006 WLPA Amendment preceded or followed the Sariska crisis. In fact, the Sariska local extinction (confirmed 2004-05) served as a catalyst for the 2006 amendment — the sequence is causal, not merely temporal. Students who do not know this causal link may place the amendment before or independent of Sariska.
solution.final_explanation:
The evolution of tiger conservation policy in India follows a traceable timeline where each milestone is causally connected to the next.

Correct sequence: I → III → II → IV

• I (1973): Launch of Project Tiger as an administrative scheme — the founding milestone.
• III (2004-05): Confirmed local extinction of tigers in Sariska Tiger Reserve due to poaching and monitoring failures — this crisis directly triggered the push for institutional reform.
• II (2006): WLPA Amendment introducing Chapter IVB — creating NTCA, mandating Tiger Conservation Plans, and providing statutory backing to Project Tiger; a direct institutional response to Sariska.
• IV (2022): All-India Tiger Estimation confirmed approximately 3,682 tigers in India — the most recent census result using camera-trap methodology.

Value Addition:
• Pugmark-based census was phased out after being discredited; camera-trap density estimation is now the standard.
• India achieved the TX2 goal (doubling tiger numbers from 2010 baseline) four years ahead of the 2022 target, by the 2018 census.
• MSTrIPES is the real-time patrol monitoring app used between census cycles — distinct from the census methodology itself.

solution.concept_anchor: Tourism prohibition in Core/CTH — non-negotiable NTCA norm
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because the 2012 Supreme Court order is a real event and students may believe the Court's subsequent modification allowed states to decide tourism rules for core zones independently.
elimination_logic: Identify the legal issue: the forest department wants to allow guided safaris in the CTH (Core Zone) — the question is whether this is permissible.
Eliminate (a): States cannot unilaterally override NTCA norms for core zones by issuing departmental orders — NTCA guidelines bind state action in CTH.
Eliminate (b): The 2012 SC order's modification allowed regulated tourism in buffer zones, not in core/CTH areas — the core zone restriction remains non-negotiable.
Eliminate (d): CTH is NOT equivalent to an ESZ — confusing these two is a classic trap; the prohibition flows from NTCA norms under WLPA, not from EPA-based ESZ rules.

Confirm (c): Tourism in the Core/CTH of any Tiger Reserve is prohibited under NTCA guidelines; only conservation-related activities are permitted — the state forest department cannot lawfully proceed.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students familiar with the 2012 Supreme Court tiger tourism controversy may recall that the Court's order was later modified to permit regulated tourism. The trap is in the word 'modified' — the modification allowed tourism to resume in buffer zones under regulated conditions, but the prohibition on tourist activity in CTH/core zones was never lifted. A student with partial knowledge of the SC ruling may select option (b) believing the state retains discretion post-modification.
solution.final_explanation:
The regulation of tourism within Tiger Reserves operates on a strict zonal basis, and the core/CTH prohibition is non-negotiable under NTCA guidelines.

Applicable principle: Under NTCA norms issued under WLPA 1972, the Core Zone (Critical Tiger Habitat) of any Tiger Reserve must remain inviolate. No tourism — including guided wildlife safaris — is permissible in the CTH. The 2012 Supreme Court ruling temporarily banned all tiger tourism; after review, regulated tourism was permitted only in buffer zones, not in core areas.

Mapping to scenario: The forest department of State X proposes guided safaris inside the CTH. This directly conflicts with the NTCA's non-negotiable prohibition on tourism in core zones.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: State forest departments cannot override NTCA guidelines by issuing departmental circulars — NTCA guidelines are issued under statutory authority.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The SC's 2012 modification restored regulated tourism in buffer zones only; core/CTH tourism prohibition was not relaxed.
• Option (c) — Correct: The activity is impermissible; NTCA norms prohibit tourism in CTH regardless of state discretion.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: ESZ rules under EPA 1986 are a separate legal instrument from CTH restrictions under WLPA — mixing these frameworks is the conflation trap.

Value Addition:
• Buffer zone tourism must follow a Tourism Master Plan prepared as part of the Tiger Conservation Plan.
• States have autonomy in regulating buffer zone tourism but no discretion in core zone tourism.
• The 2012 SC case was filed by wildlife NGOs challenging unchecked tourist presence disrupting tiger habitats.

solution.concept_anchor: CITES Appendix I scope — domestic vs. international trade
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is deceptive because the statement about 'exceptional non-commercial circumstances' is the actual rule for Appendix I trade, and a student who half-knows the rule may flag this as odd rather than (b).
elimination_logic: Option (a) is correct: Tiger (Panthera tigris) is indeed listed under CITES Appendix I — consistent with the strictest protection category.
Option (c) is correct: Appendix I permits trade only in exceptional non-commercial circumstances with both import and export permits — this is the standard Appendix I rule.
Option (d) is correct: CITES does not govern domestic trade within a country — it only regulates international commercial trade.

Option (b) is the odd one out: CITES Appendix I does NOT ban ALL use — only international commercial trade. Domestic use, captive breeding, and non-commercial scientific exchange may still occur under permit. The statement incorrectly extends CITES to all use universally.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension in option (b) is precise: students who know CITES Appendix I provides the 'strictest' protection may assume this means all trade and use is banned globally. In fact, CITES specifically governs international commercial trade; non-commercial scientific exchange, permits for exceptional circumstances, and domestic trade are separately regulated. The trap works because 'strictest prohibition' sounds synonymous with 'total ban on all use' — it is not.
solution.final_explanation:
CITES Appendix I is the highest protection tier under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species, but its scope is often misunderstood.

• Option (a): Correct — Panthera tigris (all subspecies) is listed under CITES Appendix I, reflecting the species' risk from international commercial trade.
• Option (b): This is the odd one out — CITES Appendix I does NOT ban all use of tigers; it prohibits international commercial trade. Domestic trade, non-commercial scientific exchange, and exceptional permitted uses remain possible.
• Option (c): Correct — Appendix I allows trade only in exceptional non-commercial circumstances, requiring both export and import permits from the respective CITES Management Authorities.
• Option (d): Correct — CITES is an international treaty and has no jurisdiction over trade that occurs wholly within a single country's borders. India's domestic tiger trade prohibition comes from Schedule I of WLPA 1972.

Value Addition:
• WLPA Schedule I provides equivalent domestic protection to CITES Appendix I — both apply independently to tigers in India.
• WCCB is India's designated authority for CITES implementation, not NTCA.
• India is a CITES signatory since 1976.

solution.final_explanation:
The TX2 goal and its achievement by India are frequently tested together, with the year of achievement being the critical variable.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The St. Petersburg Declaration emerged from the 2010 Tiger Summit attended by all 13 tiger range countries. The TX2 commitment was a pledge to double wild tiger numbers from the 2010 baseline (estimated ~3,200 globally) to approximately 6,000 by 2022.

Value Addition:
• TX2 is a political declaration, not a binding UN treaty — CITES remains the binding international instrument for tiger trade regulation.
• India's 2022 census (~3,682 tigers) showed continued growth but must be contextualised: India holds over 70% of the world's wild tiger population.
• Global Tiger Forum (GTF), headquartered in New Delhi, coordinates international tiger conservation efforts among member states.

The Sariska and Panna local extinctions are landmark case studies in UPSC conservation questions.

• Option (d) — Incorrect: Sariska is in Rajasthan (Alwar district), not Madhya Pradesh.

• These cases are cited as evidence for the importance of CTH inviolability and anti-poaching investment.

statement_analysis.reason: MSTrIPES (Monitoring System for Tigers — Intensive Protection and Ecological Status) was developed by WII as a standardized mobile tool for frontline patrol monitoring, feeding data into a national database.

statement_analysis.statement: The All-India Tiger Estimation conducted every four years relies primarily on MSTrIPES data to calculate tiger population size and density across reserves.
statement_analysis.reason: The All-India Tiger Estimation uses camera-trap density estimation and occupancy modelling conducted by WII — MSTrIPES is a patrol-monitoring tool between censuses, not a census instrument itself.

statement_analysis.statement: MSTrIPES is mandatory for all Tiger Reserves and forms part of NTCA's standardized monitoring framework.
statement_analysis.reason: NTCA has mandated MSTrIPES deployment across all Tiger Reserves as part of its standardized approach to continuous habitat and threat monitoring.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is deceptive because students who associate WII with both MSTrIPES and the census may believe the two tools are integrated into a single estimation system, making the 'all correct' option tempting.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct: MSTrIPES is a WII-developed patrol monitoring app — verified against its design purpose.
Statement 2 is incorrect: The tiger census uses camera-trap methodology, not MSTrIPES — MSTrIPES records patrol effort and threats, not population density data for the estimation.
Statement 3 is correct: NTCA mandates MSTrIPES across all Tiger Reserves as a standard monitoring tool.
Statements 1 and 3 are correct; Statement 2 is incorrect — the answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is the scope-extension trap: because MSTrIPES is used inside Tiger Reserves and WII conducts the census, students assume the two data streams are the same process. The critical distinction is that MSTrIPES records patrol-based field data continuously (threats, sightings, patrol effort), while the tiger census uses systematic camera-trap grid methodology with occupancy modelling — these are fundamentally different scientific methods.
solution.final_explanation:
India's tiger monitoring architecture involves two distinct systems that must not be conflated.

• Statement 1 — Correct: MSTrIPES is a mobile application developed by WII for frontline patrol monitoring. Guards record patrol routes, wildlife sightings, human pressure indicators, and threats — data that feeds into NTCA's national monitoring database.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The All-India Tiger Estimation (every 4 years) uses camera-trap density estimation and occupancy modeling methodology — not MSTrIPES data. MSTrIPES is a continuous management monitoring tool, not a scientific population estimation instrument.
• Statement 3 — Correct: NTCA has standardized MSTrIPES deployment across all Tiger Reserves, making it mandatory as part of the reserves' operational monitoring framework.

Value Addition:
• Camera-trap surveys for tiger estimation are conducted across both Tiger Reserves and outside reserve areas — a landscape-level approach.
• Pugmark-based census was phased out after the Sariska failure exposed its unreliability.
• WII is based in Dehradun and is autonomous under MoEFCC — it is NOT a statutory body under WLPA.

solution.concept_anchor: Authority to order hunting of Schedule I species — Chief Wildlife Warden only
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because the District Collector is the most visible administrative authority in rural areas where human-tiger conflicts occur, making it intuitively plausible that the Collector would have powers over such situations.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): The Forest Range Officer is a field-level functionary with no authority to direct hunting of any Schedule I species.
Eliminate (b): The District Collector handles law and order but has no wildlife law authority to order hunting of a tiger under WLPA 1972.
Eliminate (c): NTCA is a statutory body with planning and policy functions — it does not give field-level orders to hunt individual animals.
Confirm (d): Under WLPA 1972, only the Chief Wildlife Warden of the state can declare a tiger a man-eater and authorize its hunting or translocation.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: In real-world conflict situations, District Collectors often coordinate government responses and issue orders in emergencies — this administrative reality makes option (b) feel correct to students who reason from governance logic rather than wildlife law specifics. The WLPA 1972 vests this specific power exclusively in the Chief Wildlife Warden as a deliberate check, recognising that Schedule I species hunting must be authorised by a specialised wildlife official, not a general administrator.
solution.final_explanation:
The power to authorise hunting of a Schedule I species — including tigers declared as man-eaters — is tightly controlled under WLPA 1972.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Forest Range Officers are field supervisors with patrolling and enforcement duties; they have no authority under WLPA to direct hunting of Schedule I animals.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: District Collectors wield broad administrative powers but have no specific mandate under WLPA for wildlife hunting decisions — this is a classic administrative vs. wildlife law conflation.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: NTCA operates at the national policy level; hunting decisions for individual animals are a state-level operational call under state wildlife law.
• Option (d) — Correct: WLPA 1972 vests the exclusive authority to declare a tiger a man-eater and authorize its hunting or translocation in the Chief Wildlife Warden of the state.

Value Addition:
• Even after a man-eater declaration, the Chief Wildlife Warden must follow prescribed WLPA procedures before authorising lethal action.
• States must exhaust non-lethal options (tranquilisation, translocation) before considering hunting.
• Compensation for livestock loss and human casualties is paid by state governments under state-level wildlife compensation schemes — NTCA issues only advisory guidelines.

solution.concept_anchor: CEC vs. NTCA — different legal channels for Tiger Reserve oversight

statement_analysis.statement: The Central Empowered Committee (CEC) is a statutory body constituted under the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972 to oversee compliance with tiger conservation laws.
statement_analysis.reason: The CEC is a Supreme Court-appointed committee, not a statutory body. It was constituted by the Supreme Court to monitor compliance with judicial orders on forests and wildlife — it does not derive its authority from WLPA 1972.

statement_analysis.statement: Any diversion of forest land within a Tiger Reserve requires both NTCA's statutory clearance under WLPA 1972 and a separate clearance under the Forest Conservation Act, 1980.
statement_analysis.reason: Forest land diversion within Tiger Reserves requires dual clearance: NTCA's approval under WLPA (for impact on tiger habitat) and FCA 1980 clearance from MoEFCC for the forest land diversion itself.

statement_analysis.statement: NTCA can directly override state government decisions regarding Tiger Reserve management through mandatory directives that are binding under WLPA 1972.
statement_analysis.reason: NTCA can recommend, advise, and approve/reject plans, but cannot 'override' state governments through mandatory directives — it can recommend withdrawal of Tiger Reserve status but cannot directly override day-to-day state management decisions.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because students who identify only Statement 1 as incorrect (CEC is not statutory) may miss Statement 3's subtle distinction between NTCA's advisory/approval role and an outright override power.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is NOT correct: CEC is appointed by the Supreme Court, not created by any statute — this eliminates options listing only Statement 3 as incorrect.
Statement 2 is correct: Dual clearance (NTCA + FCA 1980) for forest diversion in Tiger Reserves is accurate — this cannot be in the 'NOT correct' answer.
Statement 3 is NOT correct: NTCA cannot issue binding overriding directives to state governments; it has approval, advisory, and recommendation powers — but not override authority.
Statements 1 and 3 are NOT correct — the answer is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is a plausible-fabrication trap — it sounds authoritative because students know NTCA is the apex statutory body for tiger conservation and may assume this apex status translates to override powers. However, India's federal structure means central statutory bodies cannot directly override state government decisions; NTCA's powers are carefully scoped to approvals, recommendations, and advisory functions within the cooperative federal design of WLPA.
solution.final_explanation:
The relationship between CEC, NTCA, and state governments in Tiger Reserve governance involves three distinct legal channels.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The CEC is not statutory — it was constituted by the Supreme Court to monitor compliance with SC orders on forests and wildlife. It reports to the SC, not to Parliament via MoEFCC.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Forest land diversion within Tiger Reserves requires dual clearance: NTCA under WLPA 1972 (for tiger habitat impact) and FCA 1980 clearance for the forest land diversion component.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: NTCA's powers are circumscribed — it approves TCPs, can recommend withdrawal of Tiger Reserve status, and provides advisory guidance, but it cannot issue binding override directives against state governments. India's federal structure prevents this.

Value Addition:
• CEC's role is specifically tied to Supreme Court jurisdiction — its recommendations carry the weight of court orders.
• NTCA reporting to Parliament via MoEFCC and CEC reporting to the SC represent two parallel but non-hierarchical oversight mechanisms.
• When NTCA and CEC recommendations conflict, the matter typically returns to the Supreme Court for resolution.

solution.concept_anchor: Tiger corridors — no dedicated legislation; planning construct only
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because students who know both facts independently (corridors face legal protection gaps AND cross state boundaries) may see a connection between them without verifying whether R actually explains A causally.
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is A correct? Yes. Tiger corridors have no dedicated legislation protecting them — they are management and planning constructs identified in NTCA landscape plans and TCP buffer zones, not legally designated areas.
Step 2 — Is R correct? Yes. Major tiger corridors (Terai Arc, Central Indian, Western Ghats) cross state boundaries, revenue lands, and private areas — this is factually accurate.

Step 3 — Does R explain A? Yes. The multi-jurisdictional nature of corridors (crossing state boundaries, revenue lands, and private areas) is precisely what makes dedicated national legislation difficult to frame and enforce, which is why no dedicated corridor law exists. R causally explains A.
Both A and R are correct and R explains A — the answer is (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This is one of the rarer UPSC assertion-reason designs where both A and R are correct AND causally connected. The trap is option (b) — which would be correct if the causal connection were absent. Students who automatically default to option (b) for A-R questions (because UPSC frequently uses the 'both correct but unrelated' pattern) will be caught here. The question rewards students who actually verify the causal logic rather than pattern-matching.
solution.final_explanation:
Tiger corridors represent one of the most significant unresolved gaps in India's wildlife legal framework.

Assertion (A) is correct: Tiger corridors are NOT separately designated under any law. They exist as planning constructs in NTCA's landscape-level plans and in the buffer zone components of Tiger Conservation Plans. No statute creates, protects, or governs tiger corridors as a legal category.

Reason (R) is correct: India's major tiger corridors — the Terai Arc Landscape, Central Indian Landscape, and Western Ghats Landscape — cross state jurisdictions, revenue lands, and private property. This multi-actor, multi-jurisdictional character is a well-documented feature.

Causal relationship: R explains A. The very reason a dedicated corridor legislation is absent is the jurisdictional complexity described in R — framing enforceable legal protection for linear habitats that pass through multiple states, private lands, and revenue territories requires coordinated federal action that has not yet materialised.

Value Addition:
• Corridors are critical for genetic exchange between tiger populations — their degradation leads to inbreeding and population collapse.
• The Terai Arc Landscape corridor connects reserves in Uttarakhand and UP with Nepal's Chitwan and Bardia parks.
• India's Wildlife Action Plan 2017-2031 identifies corridor protection as a priority but has not produced dedicated legislation.

solution.concept_anchor: Schedule I WLPA vs. CITES Appendix I — independent legal regimes

statement_analysis.statement: Under Schedule I of the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972, hunting of tigers is absolutely prohibited, and a Schedule I species cannot be hunted even in self-defence without a specific order from the Chief Wildlife Warden.
statement_analysis.reason: Schedule I of WLPA provides the highest domestic protection — hunting, capture, and trade are absolutely prohibited, with the narrow exception of a Chief Wildlife Warden's order for man-eaters.

statement_analysis.statement: Since tiger is listed under CITES Appendix I, India's Schedule I listing under WLPA 1972 is legally redundant — any activity regulated by CITES Appendix I is automatically covered by WLPA Schedule I and vice versa.
statement_analysis.reason: CITES Appendix I and WLPA Schedule I are independent legal regimes operating on different domains — CITES governs international commercial trade while WLPA governs all domestic activities. Neither makes the other redundant; both apply concurrently.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because both instruments protect the same species (tiger) and both provide the highest tier of protection in their respective domains, leading students to conflate them as a single harmonised system.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct: Schedule I prohibition on hunting tigers, with the sole exception of Chief Wildlife Warden orders for man-eaters, is accurate under WLPA 1972.

Statement 2 is incorrect: CITES Appendix I and WLPA Schedule I are independent legal instruments — CITES operates internationally on commercial trade; WLPA operates domestically on all wildlife interactions. Neither makes the other redundant.
Since Statement 1 is correct and Statement 2 is incorrect, the answer is (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in Statement 2 operates by overstating the relationship between two real and independently valid legal instruments. Students who know both Schedule I and Appendix I protect tigers at the highest level may extend this to conclude they are legally equivalent or mutually substitutable. The critical distinction — domestic vs. international domain — is what differentiates them, and missing this makes Statement 2 feel correct.
solution.final_explanation:
India's tiger protection operates through two parallel but legally distinct frameworks, each covering a different domain.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Schedule I of WLPA 1972 is India's domestic apex protection tier. Tigers cannot be hunted, captured, or traded within India under any circumstances except upon a specific order from the Chief Wildlife Warden (for man-eaters only). Penalty: imprisonment up to 7 years + fine.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: CITES Appendix I and WLPA Schedule I are not redundant — they govern entirely different legal spheres. CITES regulates international commercial trade between countries; WLPA regulates domestic activities (hunting, trade, capture) within India. India can domestically prohibit activities that CITES does not address, and CITES obligations do not automatically translate into domestic law without legislative action (which WLPA independently provides).

Value Addition:
• Penalty for hunting a Schedule I species was enhanced by the 2003 amendment to WLPA — minimum 3 years, maximum 7 years imprisonment.
• India's domestic tiger trade prohibition is broader than CITES — CITES bans international commercial trade; WLPA bans virtually all domestic trade regardless of commercial nature.
• WCCB coordinates CITES compliance at the international level while state wildlife departments enforce WLPA domestically.

solution.concept_anchor: Gram Sabha consent mandatory for CTH relocation — FRA 2006 + WLPA reconciliation
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because students may believe that once an area is legally notified as CTH under WLPA (an inviolate area), the conservation law automatically overrides FRA rights — reversing the correct legal position where both laws must be reconciled.
elimination_logic: Identify the legal conflict: CTH under WLPA 1972 mandates inviolate status; FRA 2006 recognizes community forest rights and requires Gram Sabha consent for relocation.
Eliminate (a): CTH notification does not extinguish FRA rights — Supreme Court interpretations require both laws to be reconciled, not one to override the other.
Eliminate (c): The District Collector has no authority to override FRA procedural requirements simply on the basis of conservation urgency — this conflates administrative and wildlife law powers.
Eliminate (d): There is no provision requiring referral to the CEC for routine relocation decisions; CEC's role relates to SC orders on forest diversion, not standard resettlement.

Confirm (b): Under FRA 2006, Gram Sabha consent is mandatory before any relocation from forest areas. The state government must complete the FRA process — including Gram Sabha consent — before proceeding with resettlement even from a CTH.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The reversed-causation trap in option (a) inverts the actual legal relationship: it implies CTH designation causes FRA rights to lapse, when the correct position is the opposite — FRA rights cannot be extinguished by CTH notification, and the FRA process must be completed before relocation. Students who know CTH is 'inviolate' may assume this inviolability has a cascading legal effect of overriding FRA, which courts have explicitly rejected.
solution.final_explanation:
The intersection of WLPA 1972 and FRA 2006 in CTH relocation is the most legally contested area in Indian tiger conservation policy.

Applicable principle: CTH under WLPA 1972 is legally inviolate — human habitation is not permitted. However, FRA 2006 recognises community forest rights that cannot be extinguished merely by CTH notification. Relocation must be voluntary, and Gram Sabha consent is a mandatory procedural requirement under FRA rules before any resettlement can proceed.

Mapping to scenario: The village located inside the notified CTH cannot be relocated until the Gram Sabha has given its free, prior, and informed consent. The state government must complete the FRA process (rights recognition, Gram Sabha resolution, voluntary resettlement package) before physically relocating families.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: CTH notification does not automatically extinguish FRA rights — this reverses the legal position established by judicial interpretations.
• Option (b) — Correct: Gram Sabha consent under FRA 2006 is mandatory; the state government must complete the FRA process, including consent, before relocating communities.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The District Collector cannot override FRA procedural requirements on grounds of conservation urgency — no such exception exists in the law.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: CEC oversight relates to SC orders on forest land diversion, not to routine relocation decisions under FRA and WLPA.

Value Addition:
• The minimum compensation for voluntary relocation is Rs. 10 lakh per family (advisory), or land-for-land.
• FRA 2006 also allows communities to remain in forest areas where co-existence is possible — relocation is only for CTH where it is scientifically deemed impossible.
• Gram Sabha resolutions under FRA are judicially reviewable — a coercive relocation can be challenged and overturned in court.

solution.concept_anchor: WII legal character — autonomous, not statutory under WLPA
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because WCCB, like WII, is associated with wildlife protection under MoEFCC, and students may confuse WCCB's statutory character with WII's autonomous (non-statutory) character.
elimination_logic: NTCA (option a): Statutory body under Section 38L of WLPA 1972 — it has a statute-derived legal identity.
WCCB (option b): Statutory body under MoEFCC for wildlife crime enforcement — statute-derived legal identity.
WII (option c): Autonomous research institution under MoEFCC, NOT established under WLPA or any wildlife statute — it is registered as a Society; this is the odd one out.

CEC (option d): Constituted by the Supreme Court (not statutory in the legislative sense) — however, among the given options, WII is the one that most clearly does NOT share the 'wildlife law statute-derived' character with NTCA and WCCB.
WII is the odd one out — it is not a statutory body under any wildlife legislation — answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap here is subtle: NTCA, WCCB, and CEC are all institutional actors in tiger conservation with distinct but verifiable legal characters. WII appears to belong naturally in this group because it is deeply involved in tiger conservation work. However, WII is an autonomous society under MoEFCC — not a statutory body created by any wildlife law. Students who group WII with NTCA as 'both WII and NTCA are under MoEFCC and work on tigers' will miss the critical legal character distinction.
solution.final_explanation:
Three of these four bodies have a statute-derived legal character; one is an autonomous institution created under a different mechanism.

• Option (a) NTCA: Statutory body under Section 38L of WLPA 1972 — belongs to the 'statute-derived' group.
• Option (b) WCCB: Statutory body under MoEFCC for wildlife crime enforcement — belongs to the 'statute-derived' group.
• Option (c) WII — This is the odd one out: WII is an autonomous institution registered as a Society under MoEFCC, headquartered in Dehradun. It is NOT established under WLPA 1972 or any wildlife statute. It conducts tiger censuses and provides technical support but has no statutory mandate under wildlife law.
• Option (d) CEC: Constituted by Supreme Court order — while not legislative-statutory, it has judicial-authority backing distinguishing it from a mere advisory body.

Value Addition:
• WII conducts tiger census in collaboration with NTCA and state governments — its technical role is immense despite its non-statutory character.
• Forest Survey of India (FSI) is distinct from WII — FSI assesses forest cover biannually; WII conducts wildlife assessments.
• WII also provides technical support to NTCA for landscape-level conservation planning.

solution.concept_anchor: WLPA sections — Section 38L NTCA, Section 38V Tiger Reserve and TCP
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is deceptive because it correctly places Tiger Reserve declaration under Section 38V but incorrectly attributes TCP preparation to the Central Government rather than the State Government, catching students who know the section number but not the actor.
elimination_logic: Section 38L of WLPA 1972 establishes NTCA — matches with description 2 (establishment of a statutory body).
Section 38V deals with Tiger Reserve declaration (by State Government on NTCA recommendation) AND the TCP mandate — it matches description 4 (declaration process).
TCP must be prepared by the State Government and approved by NTCA — this is the core procedural point for description 1.
The 2006 WLPA Amendment (Chapter IVB) provided statutory backing to Project Tiger and created the NTCA framework — matches description 3. This gives A-2, B-4, C-1, D-3 — option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap in the distractors plays on the distinction between who prepares the TCP (State Government) versus who approves it (NTCA). Students who know 'Section 38V and TCP are connected' may confuse the actor — the section mandates TCP preparation by the state, with NTCA approval. Options that correctly cite the section but assign the wrong actor to the TCP are designed to catch this partial knowledge.
solution.final_explanation:
WLPA 1972's Chapter IVB sections are regularly tested individually and in combination.

Correct matches: A-2, B-4, C-1, D-3

• Section 38L (A) — Description 2: Section 38L establishes NTCA as a statutory body, defines its composition (MoEFCC Minister as Chair, Minister of State as Vice-Chair), and sets out its powers including TCP approval.
• Section 38V (B) — Description 4: Section 38V empowers State Governments to declare Tiger Reserves on NTCA's recommendation and mandates the two-zone (CTH + Buffer) structure.
• Tiger Conservation Plan (C) — Description 1: TCP must be prepared by the State Government under Section 38V(2) and approved by NTCA — it must cover site-specific CTH management, buffer plans, relocation packages, and monitoring protocols.
• Wildlife Protection Amendment Act 2006 (D) — Description 3: The 2006 amendment inserted Chapter IVB into WLPA 1972, providing statutory backing to Project Tiger and creating the NTCA framework that replaced purely administrative control.

Value Addition:
• Chapter IVB (Sections 38L through 38Y) of WLPA 1972 is the dedicated legal framework for Tiger Reserves.
• Non-compliance with TCP requirements can be the basis for legal challenges to reserve activities.
• The 2006 amendment also introduced Critical Tiger Habitat as a formal legal concept.

solution.concept_anchor: TX2 not a UN treaty; CITES Appendix I scope limitations

statement_analysis.statement: The TX2 goal, pledged through the St. Petersburg Declaration, is a binding international treaty obligation on all 13 tiger range countries under the United Nations Framework.
statement_analysis.reason: TX2 is a political declaration, not a legally binding UN treaty. The St. Petersburg Declaration carries moral and diplomatic weight but no treaty-level enforcement mechanism.

statement_analysis.statement: CITES Appendix I listing for the tiger prohibits all international commercial trade but does not govern domestic trade within a tiger range country.
statement_analysis.reason: CITES applies only to international trade between member countries — domestic trade within a country (such as within India) is regulated by national laws like WLPA 1972, not by CITES.

statement_analysis.statement: The Global Tiger Forum (GTF), an intergovernmental body supporting tiger conservation, has its secretariat located in Geneva, Switzerland.
statement_analysis.reason: GTF's secretariat is located in New Delhi, India — not Geneva. India is a founding and leading member, and the secretariat has been based in New Delhi since the forum's establishment.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because CITES is associated with international bodies (often based in Geneva), and students may conflate the GTF secretariat location with CITES's own secretariat location (which is in Geneva).
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is NOT correct: TX2 is a political declaration, not a binding UN treaty — eliminating options that treat only Statement 3 as incorrect.
Statement 2 is correct: CITES governs international trade, not domestic trade — this cannot be in the 'NOT correct' answer.
Statement 3 is NOT correct: GTF secretariat is in New Delhi, not Geneva (Geneva hosts CITES secretariat — a geographic swap trap).
Statements 1 and 3 are NOT correct — the answer is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 uses a geographic-swap based on a plausible association: students know many international environmental bodies are headquartered in Geneva (CITES secretariat is indeed in Geneva), and may transfer this to GTF without specific knowledge. The GTF secretariat in New Delhi is a precision fact that distinguishes well-prepared candidates. Statement 1's scope-extension — elevating a political declaration to a 'binding treaty' — is a classic UPSC trap design.
solution.final_explanation:
India's international tiger conservation commitments span political declarations and binding conventions, and the distinction matters for examination purposes.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The St. Petersburg Declaration (2010) is a political commitment by 13 tiger range countries — it has diplomatic but not treaty-level legal force. CITES is the binding international instrument for tiger trade regulation.
• Statement 2 — Correct: CITES Appendix I restricts international commercial trade in tigers; domestic trade within a country falls outside CITES jurisdiction and must be regulated by national law (in India's case, Schedule I of WLPA 1972).
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The Global Tiger Forum secretariat is located in New Delhi, India — NOT Geneva. Switzerland hosts the CITES secretariat, and this geographic swap is a precision-knowledge trap.

Value Addition:
• India achieved the TX2 goal by 2018 — four years before the 2022 deadline set in the St. Petersburg Declaration.
• GTF was established in 1994, well before the 2010 St. Petersburg Declaration — a timeline trap for those who think GTF was created by the Declaration.
• CITES was signed in Washington D.C. in 1973 and entered into force in 1975.

solution.concept_anchor: Panna tiger reintroduction — source reserves Kanha and Bandhavgarh
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is deceptive because Ranthambore is the source reserve for Sariska's reintroduction, and students who conflate the two reintroduction cases will select Ranthambore for Panna as well.
elimination_logic: Panna Tiger Reserve lost its tigers by 2009 — distinct from Sariska (which lost tigers by 2004-05).
Sariska's reintroduction source was Ranthambore — this is the well-known case and NOT the answer for Panna.
Panna's reintroductions were conducted using tigers from Kanha and Bandhavgarh — both in Madhya Pradesh.
The blank requires 'Kanha and Bandhavgarh' — confirming option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap works through conflation of two reintroduction events: Sariska (2005-06 onwards, source: Ranthambore) and Panna (2009-10 onwards, source: Kanha/Bandhavgarh). Students who recall 'Ranthambore was the source for a tiger reintroduction' without anchoring it to the correct recipient reserve (Sariska, not Panna) will select option (c). The geographic proximity of Kanha, Bandhavgarh, and Panna (all in Madhya Pradesh) is the logical clue that option (b) is correct.
solution.final_explanation:
Panna Tiger Reserve's local extinction and recovery is a distinct case study from Sariska's, and the source reserves differ.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Corbett Tiger Reserve is in Uttarakhand; Panna is in Madhya Pradesh — no reintroduction sourced from Corbett.
• Option (b) — Correct: Panna received tigers from Kanha Tiger Reserve and Bandhavgarh Tiger Reserve — both located within Madhya Pradesh, making intra-state logistics feasible for the reintroduction programme.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Ranthambore is the source for Sariska's reintroduction (Rajasthan-to-Rajasthan transfer), not for Panna — a classic entity-swap distractor.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Kaziranga is an Assam reserve primarily known for one-horned rhinos — no connection to Panna's tiger reintroduction.

Value Addition:
• Panna's local extinction (by 2009) was attributed to poaching, monitoring failures, and alleged political interference — similar systemic failures as Sariska.
• Post-reintroduction recovery at Panna has been successful — tiger numbers have grown steadily since the 2009-10 reintroductions.
• Both Sariska and Panna cases reinforced the argument for NTCA independence and mandatory CTH inviolability norms.

solution.concept_anchor: ESZ not mandatory around Tiger Reserves; SC 2022 applies to NPs/Sanctuaries

statement_analysis.statement: Eco-Sensitive Zones (ESZs) declared under the Environment Protection Act, 1986 are legally distinct from Buffer Zones established under Section 38V of the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972.
statement_analysis.reason: ESZs and Buffer Zones are created under different parent statutes (EPA 1986 vs. WLPA 1972), follow different procedures, and are independently governed — they are legally separate even when they overlap spatially.

statement_analysis.statement: A 2022 Supreme Court ruling mandating a minimum 1 km Eco-Sensitive Zone applies automatically to all Tiger Reserves in addition to National Parks and Wildlife Sanctuaries.
statement_analysis.reason: The 2022 SC ruling on minimum 1 km ESZ applies to National Parks and Wildlife Sanctuaries — it does not automatically extend to Tiger Reserves, which are governed under a distinct legal framework under WLPA Chapter IVB.

statement_analysis.statement: Buffer zones of Tiger Reserves permit regulated eco-tourism and community conservation activities, but states must prepare a tourism master plan as part of the Tiger Conservation Plan.
statement_analysis.reason: Buffer zones operate on a co-existence model under WLPA 1972; regulated eco-tourism is permitted, and states must include buffer zone tourism management in the TCP submitted to NTCA.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is deceptive because students who know the 2022 SC ESZ ruling was significant may assume it has comprehensive application to all protected areas including Tiger Reserves, making the 'all three correct' option attractive.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct: ESZ (EPA 1986) and Buffer Zone (WLPA 1972) are legally distinct — different statutes, different procedures.
Statement 2 is incorrect: The 2022 SC ruling on minimum ESZ applies to National Parks and Wildlife Sanctuaries specifically — not automatically to Tiger Reserves.
Statement 3 is correct: Buffer zone eco-tourism is permitted under WLPA and must be governed by a Tourism Master Plan within the TCP.
Statements 1 and 3 are correct; Statement 2 is incorrect — the answer is (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is a scope-extension trap: students who recall the 2022 SC ruling (a widely covered judgment) may extend its applicability beyond its actual scope. The ruling specifically addressed National Parks and Wildlife Sanctuaries under the main body of WLPA — Tiger Reserves are governed by a distinct chapter (IVB) and their ESZ applicability requires separate notification, not automatic extension from the SC ruling.
solution.final_explanation:
Buffer Zones and ESZs are parallel legal constructs that must not be conflated despite their frequent geographical overlap.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Buffer Zones are created by state government notification as part of Tiger Reserve declaration under WLPA 1972; ESZs are separately notified by MoEFCC under EPA 1986. Their parent laws, procedures, and governance mechanisms are entirely distinct.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Supreme Court's 2022 judgment mandating a minimum 1 km ESZ was directed at National Parks and Wildlife Sanctuaries. Tiger Reserves have their own legal architecture under Chapter IVB, and ESZ requirements do not flow automatically from this ruling.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Buffer zones are explicitly designed for co-existence — regulated tourism and community activities are allowed. States must prepare a Tourism Master Plan integrated with the TCP, which NTCA approves.

Value Addition:
• An ESZ and a Buffer Zone can spatially overlap but will follow different rules for the same piece of land.
• ESZ declaration can take years of consultation — many Protected Areas remain without notified ESZs despite the SC mandate.
• Buffer zone tourism revenues are increasingly being used to fund anti-poaching operations — a positive externality of the co-existence model.

solution.concept_anchor: All-India Tiger Estimation conducted by WII, not NTCA or FSI
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because NTCA is the apex statutory body for tiger conservation and logically appears to be the natural conductor of a national tiger census — students who reason from institutional hierarchy rather than specific functional mandates will choose NTCA.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): Forest Survey of India assesses forest cover biannually — it is not involved in wildlife population estimation.
Eliminate (b): NTCA is the apex statutory body but does not itself conduct the census — it collaborates with and oversees WII, which actually conducts the estimation.
Eliminate (c): Ministry of Environment directly does not conduct field surveys — census work is delegated to technical institutions.
Confirm (d): The All-India Tiger Estimation is conducted by the Wildlife Institute of India (WII), in collaboration with NTCA and state forest departments — WII is the primary technical executor.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: NTCA is the most visible institution in tiger conservation and its statutory prominence makes it the intuitive answer for 'who conducts the tiger census'. However, NTCA's role is oversight, policy, and approval — the actual technical work of estimation (camera trap surveys, data analysis, occupancy modelling) is conducted by WII. This entity-swap between the policy authority (NTCA) and the technical executor (WII) is a precision-knowledge test that eliminates candidates who reason from institutional hierarchy.
solution.final_explanation:
The All-India Tiger Estimation involves multiple actors, but technical execution rests with a specific institution.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: FSI (Forest Survey of India) conducts biennial assessments of forest cover using satellite imagery — wildlife population estimation is outside its mandate.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: NTCA is the statutory authority that oversees tiger conservation and approves the census methodology, but it does not directly conduct the field surveys and data analysis.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: MoEFCC is the parent ministry with overall policy oversight, not a technical field agency conducting census operations.
• Option (d) — Correct: WII (Wildlife Institute of India), an autonomous institution under MoEFCC headquartered in Dehradun, is the primary technical body that conducts the All-India Tiger Estimation every four years using camera-trap density estimation and occupancy modelling, in collaboration with NTCA and state forest departments.

Value Addition:
• India's 2022 census (~3,682 tigers) was the largest camera-trap wildlife survey ever conducted globally.
• WII uses over 26,000 camera trap locations across the country for the estimation.
• Census frequency: every 4 years — 2006, 2010, 2014, 2018, 2022.

solution.concept_anchor: NTCA cannot override states; CEC reports to SC not Parliament

statement_analysis.statement: The National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA), being the apex statutory body for tiger conservation, can issue binding directives to state governments that override state wildlife management decisions in Tiger Reserves.
statement_analysis.reason: NTCA's powers are advisory, approval-based, and recommendatory within India's cooperative federal structure. It cannot override state governments through binding directives — it can recommend withdrawal of Tiger Reserve status but cannot compel states on day-to-day management.

statement_analysis.statement: The Central Empowered Committee (CEC) derives its authority from Supreme Court orders and reports its findings to the Supreme Court, not to Parliament.
statement_analysis.reason: The CEC was constituted by the Supreme Court to monitor compliance with its orders on forests and wildlife — it is a court-appointed body that submits reports to the SC, not to Parliament or MoEFCC.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because both NTCA and CEC are described in authoritative terms, and students may accept both statements as correct without scrutinising NTCA's actual scope of power in the federal context.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is incorrect: NTCA operates within India's cooperative federal framework — it approves plans and can recommend reserve status withdrawal but cannot issue binding overriding directives to state governments.
Statement 2 is correct: CEC is a Supreme Court-constituted body; it reports to the SC and not to any legislative or executive body.
Statement 1 incorrect + Statement 2 correct → option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Wait — the elimination logic shows Statement 1 incorrect and Statement 2 correct, which maps to option (d). Let me re-check: options are (a) Both correct, (b) Both incorrect, (c) 1 correct 2 incorrect, (d) 1 incorrect 2 correct. The correct answer should be (d), not (c). Let me correct this.
solution.final_explanation:
The scope of NTCA's powers and CEC's accountability mechanism are frequently tested together.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: NTCA's powers are carefully scoped within India's federal structure. It can approve or reject Tiger Conservation Plans, recommend withdrawal of Tiger Reserve status, and issue advisory guidelines — but it cannot issue legally binding override directives to state governments on wildlife management decisions. This is the critical limitation that UPSC tests.
• Statement 2 — Correct: CEC was constituted by the Supreme Court (not by any statute) to oversee compliance with SC orders on forest and wildlife matters. It submits findings directly to the Supreme Court — making it judicially accountable, not parliamentarily accountable like NTCA.

Value Addition:
• The distinction between NTCA (reports to Parliament via MoEFCC) and CEC (reports to SC) reflects two parallel but independent oversight mechanisms for conservation governance.
• When the same Tiger Reserve land diversion case involves both CEC and NTCA, they operate through separate legal channels — SC route and statutory route respectively.
• NTCA's 'recommendation to withdraw Tiger Reserve status' is its strongest tool against non-compliant states — short of court intervention.

solution.concept_anchor: Tiger corridors — no dedicated legislation, planning construct only
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is deceptive because WII prepares landscape-level conservation plans that identify corridors, and students may mistake this planning role for a formal 'gazette notification' mechanism that provides legal protection to corridors.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): No 'Wildlife Corridors Act' exists in Indian legislation — a plausible-fabrication distractor.
Eliminate (c): WII identifies corridors in landscape plans but does not 'gazette notify' corridors as legally protected areas — corridor plans are technical, not statutory instruments.
Eliminate (d): NTCA includes corridor connectivity in TCP buffer zone planning but has no power to declare corridors as legally protected under any statute.
Confirm (b): Tiger corridors have no dedicated legal protection — they are management and planning constructs without a separate statutory category in Indian law.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (a) is a plausible-fabrication: 'Wildlife Corridors Protection Act' does not exist, but it sounds like a natural extension of India's conservation legal architecture. Students with superficial knowledge of Indian environmental law may accept this as a real statute. Option (c) is more dangerous for well-prepared students — they know WII conducts landscape planning and may conflate technical identification with legal gazette notification.
solution.final_explanation:
Despite their ecological significance, tiger corridors occupy an ambiguous position in Indian law.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: No Wildlife Corridors Protection Act exists. This is a plausible-fabrication distractor — no dedicated statute has been enacted to legally protect tiger or wildlife corridors in India.
• Option (b) — Correct: Tiger corridors are not separately designated under any legislation. They are identified in NTCA's landscape-level plans and in the buffer zone components of Tiger Conservation Plans — they are management tools, not legally protected areas.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: WII identifies corridors as part of technical landscape planning, but these identifications do not constitute gazette notifications under any statute. Corridors remain without the force of law.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: While TCPs include buffer zone planning that may encompass corridor areas, declaring corridors as legally protected under WLPA requires specific statutory provisions that do not currently exist.

Value Addition:
• India's Wildlife Action Plan 2017-2031 identifies corridor protection as a conservation priority without creating specific legal machinery.
• Corridors crossing private and revenue lands have no legal protection mechanism — landowners can legally alter land use.
• International models (e.g., Yellowstone-to-Yukon corridor) are cited as examples for what India's corridor legislation could adopt.

solution.concept_anchor: Core/CTH tourism ban — non-negotiable; states cannot deviate
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because students who know both A and R are factually true may assume the 2012 SC order (R) is the legal source of the tourism prohibition in core zones (A), when in fact A's basis is NTCA norms under WLPA — the SC order is an additional development, not the origin of the rule.
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is A correct? Yes. Tourism in the Core/CTH of Tiger Reserves is non-negotiable — states cannot permit it regardless of revenue or management arguments.
Step 2 — Is R correct? Yes. The Supreme Court did issue a 2012 order on tiger tourism; it was subsequently modified to allow regulated tourism, but only in buffer zones — not in core zones.

Step 3 — Does R explain A? No. The tourism prohibition in core/CTH zones flows from NTCA's norms under WLPA 1972 — it predates the 2012 SC order. The SC order addressed the broader question of tourist presence but the core zone prohibition's legal basis is NTCA's statutory mandate, not the 2012 judicial intervention.
Both A and R are correct but R does NOT explain A — the answer is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap here involves assuming that because the 2012 SC order and the core zone prohibition are associated in the same legal context, the SC order is the source of the prohibition. In fact, the core zone tourism ban was an NTCA norm predating the 2012 case — the SC order affirmed and reinforced this position, but it was not the original legal basis. R being a reinforcing factor is not the same as R being the causal explanation of A.
solution.final_explanation:
The core zone tourism prohibition and the 2012 SC tiger tourism case are temporally proximate but causally distinct.

Assertion (A) is correct: Tourism in the Core Zone/CTH of any Tiger Reserve is strictly prohibited under NTCA guidelines. This is a non-negotiable restriction — states have no discretion to permit tourist activity in CTH regardless of conservation arguments or revenue needs.

Reason (R) is correct: The Supreme Court issued an order in 2012 temporarily banning all tourism within core areas of Tiger Reserves following a petition by wildlife NGOs. The Court subsequently modified this to allow regulated tourism — but only in buffer zones.

Causal relationship: R does NOT explain A. The NTCA norm prohibiting core zone tourism predates the 2012 SC case. The SC order affirmed the existing position and generated the 2012 controversy, but the legal source of A is NTCA's statutory guidelines under WLPA Chapter IVB — not the 2012 judicial intervention. R is a reinforcing development, not a causal explanation.

Value Addition:
• Buffer zone tourism requires a Tourism Master Plan within the TCP, providing a structured framework for eco-tourism.
• The 2012 SC case was T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad-related proceedings in the Supreme Court.
• Core zone prohibition reflects the 'inviolate' principle underlying CTH designation.
